issues.legal_issue: A compulsory acquisition for a company’s building or work is constitutionally permissible only when that building or work serves the public purpose of the company’s industry or work.
material_facts: The amended law allowed acquisition for a building or work for a company engaged, or taking steps to engage, in an industry or work for a public purpose.
The challenge argued that the company’s industry alone needed to serve a public purpose, even if the acquired land would be used for a building or work unrelated to that purpose.
issues.conclusion: The provision is to be read as requiring the building or work itself to serve the public purpose of the company’s industry or work; so construed, it does not violate the constitutional protections for property or the right to hold property. The related amendments governing the required agreement are also valid.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 31(2) and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution, compulsory acquisition must be for a public purpose and restrictions on holding property must be reasonable. A court may consider statutory setting and circumstances to control an otherwise broad literal reading; where two constructions are possible, it should prefer the constitutionally consistent one. The Court relied on The Mysore State Electricity Board v. The Bangalore Woollen, Cotton and Silk Mills Ltd. and Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar. The construction also governs the consequential amendment to section 41, including its requirement for an agreement specifying the time and conditions for construction or execution.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_company_land: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of land for a company.
predicates.company_industry_serves_public_purpose: The company is engaged, or is taking steps to engage, in an industry or work that serves a public purpose.
predicates.building_or_work_serves_that_public_purp: The building or work for which the land is acquired serves the public purpose of the company’s industry or work.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns acquisition for a company, the authorization is valid if both the company’s industry and the proposed building or work serve a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A law validating earlier company acquisitions does not deem an acquisition to serve a public purpose when its actual purpose fails the applicable public-purpose test.
material_facts: The validating law applied to company acquisitions made before its specified cutoff and treated qualifying acquisitions as if the amended acquisition conditions had been in force when they were made.
The challenge argued that the law irrebuttably deemed every covered acquisition to be for a public purpose, even where it was not so in fact.
The Court construed the validation as available only where the acquisition actually satisfied the requirements for a public-purpose building or work.
issues.conclusion: The validating provision does not violate the constitutional requirement that compulsory acquisition be for a public purpose because it does not validate acquisitions that fail the applicable public-purpose test.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2) requires compulsory acquisition to be for a public purpose. The deeming language validates an earlier acquisition by applying the amended conditions retrospectively; it does not dispense with those conditions or make an acquisition valid if it would fail them. The validation applies to acquisitions in which the land has vested in the Government.

predicates.challenge_to_retroactive_validation: A party challenges a law that retrospectively validates earlier company land acquisitions.
predicates.earlier_company_acquisition_is_complete: The earlier acquisition is complete and the land has vested in the acquiring government.
predicates.acquired_land_serves_public_purpose: The acquisition satisfies the requirement that the building or work serve the public purpose of the company’s industry or work.

issues.definition: Retrospective validation of a completed company acquisition does not authorize it unless the acquired land serves the required public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: Retrospective validation of qualifying earlier company acquisitions does not discriminate against later acquisitions when both must satisfy the same substantive public-purpose conditions.
material_facts: The law addressed company acquisitions made before a specified cutoff, while later acquisitions were governed by the amended conditions directly.
The challenge asserted that validating the earlier acquisitions while requiring later acquisitions to meet the amended conditions created unconstitutional discrimination.
The Court held that the same substantive conditions applied to acquisitions in both periods and that the earlier acquisitions were validated only if they actually met those conditions.
issues.conclusion: The validating provision does not violate Article 14 because earlier and later acquisitions must satisfy the same public-purpose conditions.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits unreasonable discrimination. A temporal distinction in a validating law does not produce the alleged discrimination where earlier acquisitions receive validation only if they satisfy the same substantive conditions that govern later acquisitions.

predicates.article_14_challenge_to_temporal_validat: A party alleges that a law treats earlier and later company acquisitions unequally by validating only the earlier ones.
predicates.earlier_acquisitions_are_validated_only_: Earlier acquisitions receive validation only when they satisfy the substantive public-purpose conditions.
predicates.later_acquisitions_are_subject_to_the_sa: Later acquisitions must satisfy the same substantive public-purpose conditions.

issues.definition: A difference in timing alone does not amount to unconstitutional discrimination when both earlier and later acquisitions are subject to the same substantive conditions.

issues.legal_issue: A validating law that expressly operates notwithstanding court judgments can validate an earlier acquisition previously set aside if the acquisition is complete and satisfies the law’s substantive conditions.
material_facts: A court had previously set aside the acquisition notification.
The validating law expressly applied notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of a court.
The land had vested in the Government, and the acquisition was for a factory serving the public purpose of the company’s industry.
issues.conclusion: The previous judgment setting aside the acquisition does not prevent validation because the law expressly operates notwithstanding court judgments, and the completed acquisition satisfied the applicable conditions.
issues.legal_principle: A validating enactment that expressly operates notwithstanding judgments is intended to validate actions otherwise held invalid, to the extent of the enactment’s validation. It can reach an acquisition already set aside by a court where the land has vested in the Government and the acquisition satisfies the substantive conditions for validation.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_previously_set_: A party challenges an acquisition that a court previously set aside.
predicates.validating_law_expressly_overrides_court: The validating law expressly states that it operates notwithstanding court judgments or orders.
predicates.land_has_vested_in_government: The acquired land has vested in the Government.
predicates.acquisition_satisfies_public_purpose_con: The acquisition satisfies the substantive conditions requiring the acquired building or work to serve a public purpose.

issues.definition: A prior court order does not bar validation when the validating law overrides court orders, the land has vested in the Government, and the acquisition satisfies the applicable public-purpose conditions.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition for a company’s public-purpose industry serves a public purpose when binding arrangements restrict the land to that use and provide for its return if it is no longer required, without requiring government control of the company’s products.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a factory manufacturing textile machinery and parts, an industry purpose accepted as serving the public.
The agreement required the company to use the land only for the stated purpose unless the Government gave written approval for another use.
The agreement required the land to be returned if it was no longer required, and the law restricted the company’s ability to transfer it without government sanction.
The challenger argued that the agreement also had to regulate or control the company’s products.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition served a public purpose; the restrictions on use, return and transfer were sufficient, and the law did not require regulation or control of the company’s products.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 40(1)(aa), the acquired building or work must serve the public purpose of the company’s industry or work. The agreement must secure use of the land for the purpose for which it was acquired; the law does not require the Government to regulate production, distribution or prices. The Court also relied on the transfer restriction in section 44A.

predicates.company_land_acquisition_case: The acquisition is made for a company’s land use in connection with an industry or work.
predicates.company_industry_serves_public_purpose: The company’s industry or work serves a public purpose.
predicates.agreement_restricts_land_to_stated_purpo: The agreement restricts the company to using the acquired land for the stated purpose unless the Government approves another use.
predicates.agreement_requires_return_if_land_is_no_: The agreement requires the land to be returned if the company no longer needs it.

issues.definition: An acquisition for a public-purpose industry serves a public purpose when the agreement confines the land to the stated use and requires its return if it is no longer needed.

issues.legal_issue: The former owner’s intention to use land for a different public purpose does not invalidate an acquisition that is itself for a public purpose.
material_facts: The former owner intended to use the land to establish a factory but was prevented from doing so by restrictions associated with nearby military installations.
The land was acquired for another factory that the Court found would serve a public purpose.
The former owner’s objection was that land intended for one public purpose should not be acquired for another.
issues.conclusion: The former owner’s intended use does not affect the validity of an acquisition that is itself for a public purpose; an objection to whether the land should be acquired may be raised in the statutory objection process.
issues.legal_principle: The validity of an acquisition depends on whether it is required for a public purpose, not on the former owner’s intended use. An owner may object to the proposed acquisition through the procedure provided for objections, but a competing intended use does not by itself invalidate an acquisition found to be for a public purpose. The Court distinguished Province of Bombay v. Kusaldas S. Advani.

predicates.challenge_to_public_purpose_acquisition: A party challenges the validity of a compulsory acquisition said to serve a public purpose.
predicates.acquisition_serves_public_purpose: The acquisition is in fact for a public purpose.
predicates.former_owner_intended_a_different_public: The former owner intended to use the land for a different purpose that also served a public purpose.

issues.definition: A former owner’s competing public-purpose plan does not invalidate an acquisition that independently serves a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: Different treatment of public and government companies, on one hand, and private companies and individuals, on the other, in access to company-purpose acquisitions does not violate equality when the distinction is reasonably related to preventing private enrichment.
material_facts: The law permitted the relevant acquisitions for public companies and government companies but not for private companies or individuals.
The challenge argued that private companies and individuals could also undertake industries serving a public purpose and were therefore unequally treated.

The Court considered that private companies and individuals could obtain private enrichment from the acquisition, while public companies were broad-based and government companies served the public through the Government.
issues.conclusion: The distinction is justified by its relationship to the object of the law and does not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classifications with a reasonable relationship to the object sought to be achieved. The distinction between public or government entities and private individuals or companies was reasonably related to limiting private enrichment from compulsory acquisition for a company’s public-purpose industry. The Court considered sections 40(1)(aa) and 44B.

predicates.article_14_challenge_to_company_classifi: A party alleges that different eligibility for compulsory acquisition among types of companies or persons violates equality.
predicates.acquisition_is_available_to_public_or_go: The acquisition scheme makes the relevant acquisition available to public or government entities but not to private companies or individuals.
predicates.classification_is_reasonably_related_to_: The distinction is reasonably related to preventing private enrichment from the compulsory acquisition.

issues.definition: The classification does not violate equality when it reserves the relevant acquisition for public or government entities and is reasonably related to preventing private enrichment.
